sadashivrao-bhau: Sadashivrao Bhau was born on 4 August 1730 at Satara into a Marathi Chitpavan Brahmin family, the son of Chimaji Appa, younger brother of Peshwa Baji Rao I, and Rakhmabai of the Pethe family. His mother died when he was about a month old and his father when he was ten, and he was raised by his grandmother Radhabai and his aunt Kashibai. He served as a finance minister during the reign of the Maratha ruler Rajaram II.

His first campaign was in Karnataka in 1746. He won his first battle at Ajra, south of Kolhapur, and took thirty-six parganas. In a later Carnatic campaign he conquered territory from the Nawab of Savanur and put down the revolt of Yamaji Shivdev.

Having seen the effect of artillery and light guns in British hands, he built similar units for the Maratha army. In 1760 he engaged Ibrahim Khan Gardi, a former officer of the Nizam of Hyderabad, who brought 2,500 trained soldiers and fifteen cannons. Within two years the infantry and artillery division had grown to 10,000 men and 56 guns.

Appointed to lead the army to Delhi against Ahmad Shah Abdali, he set out from Patdur on 14 March 1760 with about 55,000 men and roughly 200,000 non-combatants, including families and pilgrims. Unlike Malharrao Holkar and Raghunathrao he did not know the politics of the north. He disregarded the advice of Suraj Mal, the Jat ruler of Bharatpur, to leave the civilians at Agra. The army took Delhi on 2 August 1760 and then stormed the fort of Kunjpura, killing its entire garrison.

Abdali crossed the swollen Yamuna at Baghpat between 23 and 25 October 1760, surprised the Marathas and cut their supply lines. A two-month blockade near Panipat brought famine to the camp, where many civilians and animals died. On 14 January 1761 the Marathas tried to break out. After his nephew Vishwasrao, the Peshwa's heir, was killed around 2 p.m., Sadashivrao reportedly left his elephant and charged on horseback; the empty howdah led some troops to think him dead. He died fighting, and the remaining civilians were massacred. Some records say his headless body was recovered three days later, others that it was never found.

His widow Parvatibai, who had accompanied the campaign, refused the conventional life of widowhood. Around 1770 a man appeared in Pune claiming to be Sadashivrao; he was exposed and became known as Totayaa, the impostor. The Sadashiv Peth quarter of Pune is named after him.
saint-petersburg: Saint Petersburg lies in the middle taiga lowlands along the shores of the Neva Bay of the Gulf of Finland, at the head of the Baltic Sea, and on the islands of the Neva delta. The largest of these are Vasilyevsky Island and Petrogradsky Island. In the south the city crosses the Baltic-Ladoga Klint and meets the Izhora Plateau. Before the 17th century the area was inhabited by the Finnic Izhorians and Votians, and Ingrian Finns moved there from Karelia and Savonia under Swedish rule.

Swedish colonists built the fortress of Nyenskans at the mouth of the Neva in 1611, and the small town of Nyen grew up around it. At the end of the 17th century Peter the Great wanted a seaport to trade with the rest of Europe, since the main one, Arkhangelsk on the White Sea, was closed to shipping in winter. On 12 May 1703 (1 May, old style), during the Great Northern War, he captured Nyenskans. On 27 May 1703 (16 May, old style), he laid down the Peter and Paul Fortress on Zayachy Island, the first brick and stone building of the new city. It was named after the apostle Saint Peter.

The city served as the capital of the Tsardom of Russia and of the Russian Empire from 1712 to 1918, except around 1728 to 1730, when Moscow replaced it. After the October Revolution in 1917 the Bolsheviks moved their government to Moscow. The city was renamed Petrograd and then Leningrad after Lenin's death in 1924. It was the site of the siege of Leningrad in World War II, the most lethal siege in history. In June 1991 voters supported restoring the original name, which took effect on 1 October 1991.

The first Russian railway was built there in 1837. The Kunstkamera, whose collection Peter the Great established in 1714 to gather curiosities from around the world, is sometimes considered the first museum in Russia. In 1914 an international chess tournament, partly funded by Tsar Nicholas II, was the first at which the title Grandmaster was formally conferred, on Lasker, Capablanca, Alekhine, Tarrasch and Marshall.

Saint Petersburg is the second-largest city in Russia, with 5,601,911 residents in the 2021 census, and is governed as a federal city. Its historic centre, mostly Baroque and Neoclassical buildings of the 18th and 19th centuries, has been largely preserved. The Historic Centre of Saint Petersburg and Related Groups of Monuments have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1991. The city has more than two hundred museums, the largest being the Hermitage, which occupies the former imperial residence.
samnite-wars: The Samnites were a confederation of four tribes living in the mountains east of Campania. Rome and the Samnites made a treaty in 354 BCE whose terms are not recorded; modern historians have proposed that it made the River Liris the boundary between their spheres. Livy, the only continuous source for the first war, says it began when the Samnites attacked the Sidicini and then the Campanians, and Capua surrendered itself to Rome. Modern historians doubt his three Roman victories of 343 BCE. The war ended in 341 BCE in a negotiated peace: Rome accepted that the Sidicini lay in the Samnite sphere but kept its alliance with the Campanians.

The second war grew out of Roman moves in Campania: a colony founded at Fregellae in 328 BCE and the taking of Naples in 326 BCE. In 321 BCE the consuls Titus Veturius Calvinus and Spurius Postumius Albinus were trapped by the Samnite commander Gaius Pontius in the Caudine Forks and surrendered; their soldiers passed unarmed under the yoke and six hundred equites were given as hostages. Livy says Rome rejected the agreement and avenged it, a claim some modern scholars doubt. Fighting resumed in 316 BCE, and in 304 BCE, after the fall of Bovianum, the Samnites sought peace; Livy says the old treaty was restored.

The third war began in 298 BCE, when the Lucanians asked for Roman protection against Samnite invasion. In 295 BCE Rome faced a coalition of Samnites, Etruscans, Umbrians and Senone Gauls. At Sentinum the consul Publius Decius Mus devoted himself, charging into the enemy line to his death, and Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus won the battle; Livy gives 8,700 Roman dead and 20,000 of the enemy. Livy's surviving narrative ends in 293 BCE, and the last campaigns to 290 BCE are known only in outline.

The Samnites were forced to become allies of Rome, on terms that must have been unequal, and a colony was planted at Venusia in south-eastern Samnia. Gaius Pontius was captured, paraded in a triumph and beheaded. Around Samnia Rome had already bound the Marsi, Marrucini, Paeligni and Frentani by alliance in 304 BCE and the Vestini in 302 BCE, and it annexed the Hernici and the Sabines by giving them citizenship without the vote. The allies supplied soldiers at their own expense and shared the spoils, which greatly enlarged the manpower Rome could call on.
sandzak: Sandžak covers around 8,500 square kilometres between the south-eastern border of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the borders with Kosovo and Albania. Six of its municipalities are in Serbia (Novi Pazar, Sjenica, Tutin, Prijepolje, Nova Varoš and Priboj) and seven in Montenegro (Pljevlja, Bijelo Polje, Berane, Petnjica, Rožaje, Gusinje and Plav). The name is the Serbo-Croatian form of the Ottoman Turkish sancak, a province; Serbs have historically known the region as Raška, of which it was part in the 12th century.

The Ottoman Empire invaded the Serbian Despotate in 1455. The spread of Islam in Sandžak had several causes: Muslims did not pay the jizya tax or the child levy and were privileged over Christians in administration and the courts; after the Great Turkish War (1683–1699) part of the Orthodox population was driven north and the land was settled by people who were or became Muslim; and the region was a centre of trade. Until 1790 it belonged to the Sanjak of Bosnia, which is why its Muslims identify with the Slavic Muslims of Bosnia.

When Serbian and Montenegrin troops seized the region in October 1912, many Slavic Muslims and Albanians left for Ottoman Turkey. In 1919 an Albanian revolt in the Rožaje, Gusinje and Plav districts against inclusion in the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes was put down; seven hundred Albanians were killed in Rožaje and about 450 civilians in Plav and Gusinje.

In 1941 the region was partitioned between Italian-held Montenegro, the Italian protectorate of Albania and German-occupied Serbia, and Muslim militias, Chetniks and Partisans fought there. On 2 March 1942 the Jews of Novi Pazar were rounded up and killed in camps. In May 1943 Chetnik forces under Pavle Đurišić massacred an estimated 5,400 Albanian men, women and children in Bihor, and an estimated 9,000 Muslims in all were killed by Chetniks and affiliated groups during the war. A Partisan council for Sandžak, founded at Pljevlja on 20 November 1943, accepted on 29 March 1945 the division of the region along the line of 1912.

The municipalities of Sandžak have around 361,656 inhabitants. Bosniaks form 54.8 per cent, Serbs 30 per cent, Montenegrins 5 per cent, people who declare themselves Muslims by ethnicity 3.4 per cent and Albanians 1 per cent. Novi Pazar is the economic and cultural centre. A referendum on autonomy organised by the Muslim National Council of Sandžak between 25 and 27 October 1991 was declared illegal by Serbia. The region remains underdeveloped, and census data show emigration by all its peoples.
santiago: Santiago lies in the centre of the Santiago Basin, a flat, bowl-shaped valley of fertile land surrounded by mountains. The main chain of the Andes flanks it to the east and the Chilean Coastal Range to the west, with the Cordón de Chacabuco to the north. The basin measures about 80 kilometres north to south and 35 kilometres east to west, and the Mapocho River flows through the city. A few island hills, among them Cerro Santa Lucía, rise from the plain. The historic centre, the Plaza de Armas, lies at 565 metres.

Archaeological evidence suggests that the first human groups reached the basin around the 10th millennium BCE, nomadic hunter-gatherers who travelled from the coast to hunt guanacos during the Andean snowmelt. By around 800 CE the first permanent settlers had established agricultural communities along the Mapocho, growing maize, potatoes and beans. The villages of the Picunche, whom the Incas called the Promaucae, were under Inca rule from the late 15th century to the early 16th, and the Incas placed a settlement of mitimas in the valley.

The conquistador Pedro de Valdivia, sent by Francisco Pizarro from Peru, arrived in the Mapocho valley on 13 December 1540, after a long journey from Cusco. He founded the city as Santiago del Nuevo Extremo on 12 February 1541, naming it for his home region of Extremadura and for James the Great, patron saint of Spain. It was to be the capital of his governorship of Nueva Extremadura.

The city consolidated as the capital of the Captaincy General of Chile despite food shortages, Indigenous attacks, floods and devastating earthquakes, notably in 1647. It remained the political centre during the Chilean War of Independence, which began with the First Government Junta in 1810 and ended in patriot victory at the Battle of Maipú in 1818. The Universidad de Chile traces its roots to 1622, and the 19th century brought railway construction and major educational and cultural institutions.

Santiago is the capital and largest city of Chile, and its metropolitan area holds over a third of the national population. The presidential palace, the Palacio de La Moneda, stands there, while the National Congress meets mainly in nearby Valparaíso. Few colonial buildings survive because earthquakes regularly strike the country, among them the Church of San Francisco of 1586 and the Casa Colorada of 1769. Its cathedral on the Plaza de Armas was built between 1784 and 1805 under the architect Joaquín Toesca.
sao-paulo: São Paulo stands on a plateau beyond the Serra do Mar, part of the Brazilian Highlands, at an average elevation of about 799 metres above sea level and only some 70 kilometres from the Atlantic. Two highways, the Anchieta and the Imigrantes, descend the range to the port of Santos. The Tietê River and its tributary the Pinheiros once supplied fresh water and leisure but became heavily polluted by industrial effluent in the later 20th century. The municipality covers 1,521.11 square kilometres.

The oldest archaeological artefacts found in the municipality come from the Morumbi site and are thought to date from about 3500 BCE. In 1532 Martim Afonso de Sousa founded São Vicente, the first Brazilian village, on the coast. The village of São Paulo dos Campos de Piratininga dates from 25 January 1554, when Jesuit priests founded the Colégio de São Paulo de Piratininga to catechise the indigenous peoples. The college of twelve priests included Manuel da Nóbrega and José de Anchieta, and they built a mission on a steep hill between the Anhangabaú and Tamanduateí rivers.

In the colonial period the city was the centre and starting point of the expeditions of the Paulista bandeirantes, settlers who pushed the country's territorial and economic expansion. Its wealth was consolidated in the Brazilian coffee cycle of the mid-19th century. The First and Second World Wars and the Great Depression hit coffee exports and forced rich growers to invest in industry, which drew immigrants, mainly from Italy, and migrants from the north-east. The population grew to 8.5 million inhabitants in 1980.

In 1960 the city passed Rio de Janeiro as the most populous in Brazil. Landmark events of Brazilian history took place there, among them the Cry of Ipiranga, the Modern Art Week, the 1932 Revolution and the Diretas Já movement.

São Paulo is the capital of the state of São Paulo and the largest city in Brazil, with 11,244,369 people at the 2010 census and a metropolitan area of more than 20 million. Portuguese is the main language. The city is known as the most multicultural in Brazil, with the largest Arab, Italian and Japanese communities in the world, and neighbourhoods such as Bixiga, Bom Retiro and Liberdade.
sarissa: A sarissa had two main parts, a long wooden shaft and a metal tip; some may also have had a metal butt at the other end, with which the weapon could be stood in the ground without damage to the shaft. Ash, which is long, flexible and light, and cornel wood, which is shorter but stronger, are the likeliest woods. It replaced the considerably shorter dory.

Ancient writers agree that its length set it apart, but not on the figure: Theophrastus, a contemporary of Alexander the Great, puts the longest at 12 cubits, and Polybius gives 16 cubits in the original design, reduced in practice to 14. In modern units this suggests about 5.8 m in Alexander's time and perhaps 6.3 m later.

The weapon needed both hands, so the phalangite carried only a smaller shield, the pelta, perhaps hung from a neck strap. On the march the sarissas were held upright; levelled for battle, fully five rows of points projected in front of the first rank, while the rear ranks held theirs angled upward, which also deflected arrows. A phalanx so formed was considered practically invulnerable from the front, but it turned with difficulty, and a soldier out of formation had to fall back on a sword or dagger.

Sarissa-armed phalanxes were vital in the early battles of Alexander, including the Battle of Gaugamela, though in his later campaigns he gradually reduced their importance. The surest way to beat such a phalanx was to break its formation or outflank it, as the Romans did at the Battle of Cynoscephalae in 197 BCE. A light cavalry unit of Alexander's army, the sarissophoroi, carried somewhat shorter versions; Nicholas Victor Sekunda argues that the Macedonian cavalry spear is better classed as a xyston.

A leaf-shaped spearhead 51 cm long, found by Manolis Andronikos in a Macedonian tomb at Vergina, shaped much scholarship between 1970 and 2000, but more recent work doubts that it belonged to a sarissa; Sekunda favours a small diamond-shaped iron tip of about 13.5 cm. Earlier estimates put the weight at 5.5 to 6.5 kg, yet Peter Connolly reconstructed a pike 5.8 m long in cherry wood that weighed only 4.05 kg. Scholars also draw on later pikemen, such as the Swiss and the German Landsknecht: preserved English pikes are 5.6 to 5.9 m long, which suggests that the lengths reported for the Macedonian weapon were workable.
schmalkaldic-league: The League was officially established on 27 February 1531 as a defensive religious alliance: its members pledged to defend each other if Emperor Charles V attacked their territories. At the insistence of the Elector of Saxony, membership was conditional on agreement to the Lutheran Augsburg Confession or the Reformed Tetrapolitan Confession. Unlike earlier alliances such as the League of Torgau it had a substantial military, the members agreeing to provide 10,000 infantry and 2,000 cavalry for their mutual protection.

Its formation, together with the advance of Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent in 1532, led Ferdinand of Austria to grant a religious peace, concluded at Nuremberg on 23 July 1532. Supporters of the Reformation obtained religious liberty until the meeting of a council.

In December 1535 the League opened itself to anyone who subscribed to the Augsburg Confession, and Anhalt, Württemberg, Pomerania and the cities of Augsburg, Frankfurt am Main and Kempten joined. It allied with Denmark-Norway in 1538 and gained the Electoral Palatinate in 1545. The members rarely provoked Charles directly, but they confiscated church land, expelled bishops and Catholic princes and helped spread Lutheranism through northern Germany. Martin Luther attended the meeting of 1537, for which he prepared the Smalcald Articles; they were not formally adopted then but entered the Book of Concord in 1580.

For fifteen years the League met no opposition, because Charles was at war with France and the Ottoman Empire. Francis I of France, though he persecuted Protestants at home, supported the princes from 1535 until the Treaty of Crépy in 1544. Once at peace, Charles turned on the League. In the Schmalkaldic War of 1546–1547 its leaders could not agree on a plan of battle; on 24 April 1547 the imperial forces routed them at the Battle of Mühlberg, and Philip of Hesse surrendered in May. Reformers such as Martin Bucer fled to England.

In 1548 Charles forced the League to accept the Augsburg Interim. A Protestant victory in the Second Schmalkaldic War in 1552 made him flee across the Alps, and Ferdinand signed the Peace of Passau, which granted some freedoms to Protestants. Three years later the Peace of Augsburg gave Lutheranism official status in the Holy Roman Empire and let princes choose the religion of their domains, by the principle of cuius regio, eius religio.
scholar-officials: The Chinese term, shi dafu, joins two ranks that were once distinct. In the order ascribed to the Duke of Zhou under the Western Zhou dynasty, the dafu were aristocrats who served as officers, and the shi stood between them and the ordinary people and could hold only low offices. During the Warring States period, as states annexed one another and bureaucracies grew, talented shi gave valuable service to their lords and gained influence, while dafu became an office and ceased to be a hereditary rank. The two merged. In the scheme of the Four Occupations the scholar-officials stood first, above farmers, artisans and merchants.

From the Han dynasty to the end of the Northern and Southern dynasties, officials were chosen through the recommendatory and nine-rank systems, and came mostly from prominent clans such as the Wang clan of Langya and the Cui clan of Qinghe, which supplied officials for generations and intermarried with one another and with the imperial family. The civil service examination was officially established in 587 under the Sui dynasty. In the early Tang dynasty Empress Wu Zetian reformed it by instituting a metropolitan examination, whose graduates were called jinshi; candidates were tested on poems and essays.

The Song dynasty is described as the golden age of the class. Examination had become the main path to office and the bureaucracy replaced the aristocracy. The Song was also the only dynasty to grant scholar-officials a judicial privilege: one who committed a crime faced internal impeachment in place of the ordinary courts, and for a lesser offence only a reprimand. Under the Yuan, Ming and Qing dynasties the fixed form of the eight-legged essay dominated the examinations, and the political climate left officials less free to speak and write. The Qing government abolished the examinations in 1905, and the class gradually disappeared.

Only a few degree-holders became court or local officials. Most stayed in their villages and towns as social leaders: they taught in private schools, organised welfare, helped settle minor disputes, supervised community projects, kept local order, conducted Confucian ceremonies and assisted in collecting taxes. The district magistrate, who was barred from serving in his home district, depended on them for advice, which gave them power to benefit themselves and their clients. In Confucian theory ministers were not mere subordinates and might oppose an unfit ruler. The system offered a path of upward mobility but had no formal safeguard against corruption beyond the moral teaching it examined.
scotland: The mainland of Scotland makes up the northern third of the island of Great Britain, with a total area of 30,977 square miles (80,231 km2). Its only land border, with England, runs for 96 miles (154 km) between the basin of the River Tweed and the Solway Firth. The mainland is divided into the Highlands, a mountainous region in the north and north-west, the Lowlands, a flatter plain across the centre, and the Southern Uplands along the border. Ben Nevis, at 4,413 feet (1,345 m), is the highest peak of the British Isles.

The earliest known evidence of people in Scotland is stone tools of the Hamburgian culture, made by hunter-gatherers who arrived around 14,500 to 14,000 years ago, soon after the ice sheet retreated. Neolithic farmers came about 6000 years ago. Skara Brae on Orkney, the Callanish Stones on Lewis and Maes Howe on Orkney belong to this period, the stone monuments of the third millennium BCE. The Greek sailor Pytheas made the first written reference in 320 BCE, calling the northern tip of Britain Orcas.

The Roman governor Agricola invaded in 79 CE and defeated a Caledonian army at the Battle of Mons Graupius in 83 CE, but within three years the Roman armies had withdrawn to the Southern Uplands. Under Trajan, who reigned from 98 to 117, Roman control had lapsed to the south of a line between the River Tyne and the Solway Firth, where Hadrian later built his wall. The Kingdom of Scotland emerged as a sovereign state in the 9th century and kept its independence from England partly through an alliance with France.

Its extent was largely fixed by the Treaty of York of 1237 with England and the Treaty of Perth of 1266 with Norway. Orkney and Shetland were acquired from Norway in 1472, and Berwick-upon-Tweed was ceded to England in 1482. James VI succeeded to the English and Irish thrones in 1603, and on 1 May 1707 Scotland and England combined as the Kingdom of Great Britain.

Scotland is a country within the United Kingdom, with Edinburgh as its capital and Glasgow as its largest city. The census of 2022 counted 5,436,600 people. A Scottish Parliament was re-established in 1999 with devolved authority over many areas of domestic policy. Scotland keeps its own legal system, education system and religious history. English and Scots are the most widely spoken languages, while Scottish Gaelic is spoken natively mainly in the Hebrides. Its seven World Heritage Sites include St Kilda, the Old Town and New Town of Edinburgh, New Lanark and the Antonine Wall.
second-world-war: The causes of the war included unresolved tensions after the First World War and the rise of fascism in Europe and militarism in Japan. Under the Treaty of Versailles Germany lost around 13 per cent of its home territory and all its overseas possessions, and had reparations imposed and its armed forces limited. Benito Mussolini's fascist movement seized power in Italy between 1922 and 1925, and Adolf Hitler became chancellor of Germany in 1933. Earlier events included Japan's invasion of Manchuria in 1931, Italy's invasion of Ethiopia from October 1935, the Spanish Civil War, in which Germany and Italy backed General Francisco Franco's Nationalists, and the Second Sino-Japanese War from July 1937.

The war began on 1 September 1939, when Nazi Germany invaded Poland, and the United Kingdom and France declared war on Germany on 3 September. The Soviet Union invaded Poland on 17 September, and the two states partitioned it. In 1940 Germany conquered Norway, Denmark, Belgium, Luxembourg and the Netherlands, and France fell in June. In June 1941 Germany invaded the Soviet Union. In December 1941 Japan attacked American and British territories, including Pearl Harbor, and the United States entered the war. Japan's advance was halted at the Battle of Midway in June 1942.

In early 1943 the Axis were defeated in North Africa and at Stalingrad. In 1944 the Western Allies landed in Normandy while the Soviet Union advanced into Central Europe. Germany surrendered unconditionally on 8 May 1945. The United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki on 6 and 9 August, and Japan signed a surrender document on 2 September 1945.

An estimated 60 million to more than 75 million people died, a majority of them civilians. About 6 million Jews were killed in the Holocaust, together with millions of Slavs and over 130,000 Romani. Germany lost a quarter of its pre-war territory and nine million Germans were expelled from the eastern provinces. German and Japanese leaders were tried for war crimes. The United Nations came into being on 24 October 1945, and the Soviet Union and the United States emerged as rival superpowers, setting the stage for the Cold War. The weakened great powers of Europe saw the decolonisation of Africa and Asia follow, and Italy lost its monarchy and colonial empire.
senegal: Senegal lies on the western coast of Africa between latitudes 12° and 17°N. It almost completely surrounds the Gambia, which separates the southern region of Casamance from the rest of the country. The landscape consists mainly of the rolling sandy plains of the western Sahel, rising to foothills in the southeast, where the highest point, the Baunez ridge, reaches 648 metres. The Senegal River forms the northern border and gives the country its name, and the Gambia and Casamance rivers also cross it. The capital Dakar lies on the Cap-Vert peninsula, the westernmost point of continental Africa. The dry season runs from December to April, with hot, dry harmattan winds.

Archaeological findings indicate that Senegal was inhabited in prehistoric times and continuously occupied by various ethnic groups. Kingdoms were created between the 6th and 14th centuries, among them Takrur in the 6th century, Namandiru and the Jolof Empire in the 13th and 14th centuries, and eastern Senegal was once part of the Ghana Empire. Islam was introduced by the Toucouleur and Soninke through contact with the Almoravid dynasty, and the Serers in particular resisted it. Between 1300 and 1900 close to one-third of the population was enslaved, typically after capture in warfare.

The Jolof Empire grew more powerful in the 14th century, uniting Cayor and the kingdoms of Baol, Siné, Saloum, Waalo, Futa Tooro and Bambouk. It was a voluntary confederacy rather than a state built on conquest, founded by Ndiadiane Ndiaye, and it collapsed around 1549 after the defeat and death of Lele Fouli Fak at the hands of Amari Ngone Sobel Fall.

The Portuguese landed on the coast in the mid-15th century, followed by traders from other countries, including the French. In 1677 France gained control of the island of Gorée, a minor hub of the Atlantic slave trade. From the 1850s the French expanded onto the mainland under Governor Louis Faidherbe, taking over all the kingdoms except the Serer kingdoms of Sine and Saloum. Senegal became independent in 1960.

Dakar is the capital and largest city, and was once the capital of all French West Africa. Senegal is a semi-presidential republic. French is the official language, ratified in 1960, but over 30 languages are spoken, and Wolof is the most widely spoken, serving as a lingua franca alongside French. The largest ethnic groups are the Wolof, Fula and Serer, and Senegalese people are predominantly Muslim. Griots, whose profession is passed down through generations, have kept West African history alive through words and music. Senegal is a member of the African Union, the United Nations and the Economic Community of West African States.
seoul: Seoul lies in the north-west of South Korea, in mountainous and hilly terrain, with Bukhansan on its northern edge. The Han River roughly divides it into northern and southern halves, and the city proper covers 605.25 square kilometres. Four main mountains stand in the centre: Bugaksan, Inwangsan, Naksan and Namsan. The Seoul Fortress Wall, which historically bounded the city, runs over these heights.

People lived in the area 30,000 to 40,000 years ago. Around 4,000 BCE they lived in huts with lowered floors called umjip, and around 1,500 BCE communities began to farm at scale and enter the Bronze Age. After the fall of Wiman Joseon (194 to 108 BCE), refugees went south to the Han River basin, bringing the culture and technology of the Chinese Warring States and speeding the region's entry into the Iron Age.

Baekje, founded in 18 BCE as one of the statelets of the Mahan confederacy, became the dominant local power by the 2nd century CE. Its capital, Wiryeseong, is believed to have lain in what is now south-eastern Seoul, though its exact site is uncertain. In July or August 553 Silla took the region from Baekje, and it became part of the new Sin Province. Later names include Bukhansan-gun under Goguryeo, Namgyeong under Goryeo and Hanseong under Joseon.

Seoul was designed as a capital in the late 14th century, and the Joseon dynasty built the Five Grand Palaces there: Changdeokgung, Changgyeonggung, Deoksugung, Gyeongbokgung and Gyeonghuigung. In the early 20th century the city was occupied by the Empire of Japan. In the Korean War it changed hands four times and was left mostly in ruins, and it has since been rebuilt and rapidly urbanized.

Seoul is the capital and largest city of South Korea, with about 9.6 million residents. It is divided into 25 districts, called gu. The Constitutional Court of Korea declared in 2004 that Seoul must remain the national capital as an unwritten constitutional custom, though many ministries have moved to Sejong City. Five UNESCO World Heritage Sites lie in the Seoul Capital Area, among them Changdeokgung, Jongmyo and the Royal Tombs of the Joseon dynasty.
serbia: Serbia lies in the Balkans and the Pannonian Basin. It covers 88,499 square kilometres including the disputed territory of Kosovo, or 77,589 square kilometres excluding it. It has eight neighbouring countries, more than any other European country except Germany. The Pannonian Plain covers the northern third of the country, central Serbia is chiefly hills traversed by rivers, and mountains dominate the southern third.

Elevation ranges from 2,169 metres at the Midžor peak in the Balkan Mountains to just 17 metres near Prahovo in the Timok Valley. Karst topography is prominent in the Dinaric Alps and the Carpathian Mountains, and the country hosts about 1,500 deep caves.

A hominid jaw fragment from Mala Balanica Cave is believed to be up to 525,000 years old. Around 6500 BCE the Starčevo and Vinča cultures were present near modern Belgrade, and Lepenski Vir and Vinča-Belo Brdo lie along the Danube. The Celtic Scordisci settled the area in the 3rd century BCE and built fortified settlements, including Singidunum (present-day Belgrade) and Naissos (present-day Niš). The Romans conquered much of the territory from the 2nd century BCE, and some historians believe 18 Roman emperors were born there, among them Constantine the Great.

Slavs migrated into Byzantine territory in large numbers by the 6th century. The first Serbian proto-state was established in the 7th century and had become a more stable principality by the beginning of the 9th century, remaining a Byzantine vassal state throughout. It was conquered and annexed by the Byzantine Empire in the late 10th century. The Serbian Kingdom lasted from 1217 to 1346, followed by the Serbian Empire from 1346 to 1371 and the Serbian Despotate from 1402 to 1459.

Serbia is a parliamentary republic under a constitution adopted in 2006, after the dissolution of the State Union of Serbia and Montenegro. The National Assembly has 250 deputies elected for four years. The 2022 census counted a population of 6,647,003, excluding Kosovo, of whom 80.6% were Serbs; Hungarians (2.8%) and Bosniaks (2.3%) are the largest minorities.

The country has five World Heritage sites, among them Stari Ras, the Studenica Monastery and the Roman palace complex of Felix Romuliana, and six traditions on the intangible heritage list, including the slava and kolo dance. Its cultural identity was shaped by its position as a frontier between the Byzantine Empire and Western Christianity, and later between the Ottoman and Habsburg empires.
sextus-pompey: Sextus Pompeius Magnus Pius was the son of Pompey by his third wife, Mucia Tertia, with an elder brother, Gnaeus Pompeius, and a sister, Pompeia. When Julius Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE, Gnaeus followed their father to the East while Sextus stayed in Rome in the care of his stepmother, Cornelia Metella. After the defeat at the Battle of Pharsalus in 48 BCE the two met Pompey on Lesbos and fled with him to Egypt, where Sextus watched his father killed by treachery on 29 September of that year.

He then joined the resistance to Caesar in the African provinces alongside Metellus Scipio, Cato the Younger and his brother. Caesar defeated the Pompeius brothers at the Battle of Munda in Hispania in 45 BCE. Gnaeus died soon afterwards in a last stand at Lauro; Sextus escaped and raised another army in Spain.

After Caesar's death Mark Antony moved that Sextus be recalled, paid 50 million Attic drachmas for his father's confiscated property and given command of the whole Roman navy. He accepted, but went no further than Massilia before returning to Sicily. When the Second Triumvirate began its proscriptions, many of the proscribed fled to him, and after the battles of Philippi in 42 BCE survivors of the party of Brutus and Cassius did the same. With the whole island as his base he built an army and a strong navy.

In 40 BCE his admiral, the freedman Menas, seized Sardinia from Octavian's governor Marcus Lurius. By the Pact of Misenum in 39 BCE the triumvirs recognised his control of Sicily and Sardinia in exchange for keeping the grain supply to Rome open and his pirates in check. The peace was short. Each side accused the other of breaking it, and Menas betrayed Sardinia to Octavian. Sextus defeated Octavian at sea off Messina in 37 BCE.

Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa spent a winter building and training a fleet near Lake Avernus. He fought Sextus at Mylae in August 36 BCE, Marcus Aemilius Lepidus and Titus Statilius Taurus invaded Sicily, and after Naulochus Sextus fled to Asia Minor. Captured in 35 BCE, he was put to death without trial at Miletus by Marcus Titius, whom he had once spared, either on Titius's own initiative or possibly on the orders of Antony or Plancus. Plutarch gives him a minor role in the fall of the Republic; Appian treats him as a central figure who might even have emerged as the final victor.
seychelles: Seychelles is an archipelago of 115 islands in the Indian Ocean, with its capital and largest city, Victoria, about 1,500 kilometres east of mainland Africa. The islands lie northeast of Madagascar. The inner islands, 42 granitic and 2 coralline, occupy the shallow Seychelles Bank and hold 54% of the land area. The granitic islands rest on a submerged granite block, the Seychelles microcontinent, which lay between Madagascar and India before the breakup of Gondwanaland. Alfred Wegener cited this granite as evidence of continental drift.

The islands were uninhabited before sustained outside contact. Arab sailors knew of them through Indian Ocean trade routes, and scholars identify them with the Zarin islands described by al-Mahri. Europeans learnt of them in the early 16th century. The first sighting was made on 15 March 1503 by Thomé Lopes, during Vasco da Gama's fourth Portuguese India Armada. The earliest recorded landing was in January 1609, by the crew of the Ascension under Captain Alexander Sharpeigh, on a voyage of the British East India Company.

France began to take control in 1756, when Captain Corneille Nicholas Morphey laid a Stone of Possession on Mahé. The islands were named after the French politician Jean Moreau de Séchelles and formed part of the colony of Isle de France. In August 1770 the ship Thélémaque landed 15 white settlers and 13 African and Indian slaves on Ste. Anne Island. Enslaved Africans were then brought to work the plantations.

In 1794 the senior administrator, Jean-Baptiste Quéau de Quinssy, negotiated with the British frigate HMS Orpheus and kept the islands under French control as neutral territory. Britain took control after invading Isle de France in December 1810, formalised by the Treaty of Paris of 1814. Slavery was prohibited in 1835, and indentured labourers from India were later employed. Seychelles became a separate crown colony from Mauritius in 1903. It gained independence as a republic in 1976, and a coup in 1977 ousted its first president, James Mancham.

Seychelles is a republic whose president is both head of state and head of government. French, English and Seychellois Creole are official languages, and the Creole, a French-based language, is the most widely spoken. The population was estimated at 100,600 in 2022, making it the smallest African country by area and the least populated sovereign African state. Most people descend from African, French, Indian and Chinese immigrants. It belongs to the United Nations, the African Union and the Commonwealth of Nations.
shaduf: One theory holds that the shadoof was invented in Mesopotamia as early as the time of Sargon of Akkad, around the 24th and 23rd centuries BCE. The Minoans are believed to have adopted it next, with evidence of its use from around 2100–1600 BCE. Its appearance in Upper Egypt is placed most likely in the 18th Dynasty. Some historians believe instead that the Egyptians invented it along the Nile, citing tomb drawings of shadoofs at Thebes from 1250 BCE. A third theory places its origin in India at about the same time as in Mesopotamia, because it was so widespread there, but little other evidence supports it.

The pole is hung on its frame about one-fifth of its length from one end. The vessel on the long arm may be a bucket, a skin bag or a reed basket coated with bitumen, and some have an uneven base or a tie at the top so that the water runs out at once. The operator pushes the vessel down with his own weight, and the counterweight raises it full without effort. The water is emptied into runnels that carry it along irrigation ditches. The frame may be one post or a pair, and the vessel may hang from a rope or from a thinner stick.

The device lifts water from 1 to 6 metres, and its efficiency has been calculated at 60 per cent. A study in Nigeria, which measured effort by heart rate, found that suitable adjustments reduced the energy the operator spent from about 109 to 71 watts.

In ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia shadoofs set in tiers, one above another, raised water to higher levels by the work of several people. In Egypt under the Middle and New Kingdoms, pleasure gardens watered by shadoof became a mark of luxury residences and a symbol of status. Women have often worked it, since it is easy to use.

The name comes from the Arabic šādūf; in English it is also called a well sweep or swape. The ancient Greeks knew it as the kēlōn or kēlōneion, the Chinese call it jiégāo, and its Hungarian name, gémeskút, means heron well. Today it is very common in rural India and Pakistan, and in Europe in Ukraine, Belarus, Poland and Germany. On the Great Hungarian Plain it is considered a symbol of the region.
shanghai: Shanghai lies on the Yangtze Estuary of China's east coast, with the Yangtze River to the north, Hangzhou Bay to the south and the East China Sea to the east. The Huangpu River bisects the city. The land is an alluvial plain formed by the Yangtze's deposition and by land reclamation, and most of it is flat, with an average elevation of four metres. The soil is soft, so skyscrapers have to be built on deep concrete piles to avoid sinking.

The western part of the area was inhabited 6,000 years ago. In the Spring and Autumn period it belonged to the Kingdom of Wu, which was conquered by Yue and then by Chu. The name Shanghai, on the sea, is first found in the 11th-century Song dynasty, and in 1280 the place was renamed Shanghai.

Originally a fishing village and market town, Shanghai grew to prominence in the 19th century through trade and its port. It was one of five treaty ports forced open to European trade after the First Opium War, and the Shanghai International Settlement and the French Concession were set up there. In the 1930s it was a primary commercial and financial hub of Asia. In the Second World War it fell under Japanese rule after the Battle of Shanghai, and the Communists took it during the Chinese Civil War. The reform and opening up supported by Deng Xiaoping led to extensive redevelopment by the 1990s, especially in the Pudong New Area.

Shanghai is one of the four municipalities under the direct administration of the Central People's Government and is divided into 16 districts. Its historic sites include the City God Temple, Yu Garden and the row of early 20th-century buildings along the Bund.
siege-engine: Siege engines ranged from the size of a small house to that of a large building. Some were built in place to attack from a distance, while others stood on wheels so that they could be advanced to the walls. From antiquity until the development of gunpowder they were made largely of wood, bound with rope or leather and possibly strengthened with a few pieces of metal at points of stress. Those that threw projectiles built up force by tension, by torsion or, in the trebuchet, by human power or a counterweight.

The earliest siege engines appear to be simple movable roofed towers, used with scaling ladders, depicted during the Middle Kingdom of Egypt. The Assyrians used battering rams, and in Kush siege towers and rams were built from the 8th century BCE. The Carthaginians used towers and rams against the Greek colonies of Sicily, which influenced Dionysius I of Syracuse, who developed a catapult in 399 BCE. Philip II of Macedonia and Alexander the Great were the first rulers to use siege engines to a large extent. The Helepolis of Demetrius Poliorcetes, of 304 BCE, was nine stories high, plated with iron, 40 metres tall and weighed 180 tonnes.

The Romans preferred to build earthen ramps or simply to scale the walls, their soldiers working under shelters called vineae. Roman legions first used siege towers around 200 BCE, and the onager was the main Roman invention in the field. In China the earliest documented siege artillery, a levered traction catapult and a large siege crossbow, is described in the Mozi, a Mohist text of about the 4th to 3rd century BCE.

Medieval armies used catapults such as the mangonel, the ballista, the traction trebuchet, first designed in China in the 3rd century BCE, and the counterweight trebuchet, first described by Mardi bin Ali al-Tarsusi in the 12th century though of unknown origin. Besiegers could also starve a castle out, set fires against its walls, dig mines under the foundations or throw diseased animals and human corpses over the walls to spread disease.

With gunpowder came the cannon, the petard and the mortar, which proved so effective that fortifications had to be built low and thick, as in the designs of Vauban. Specialised siege artillery culminated in the two world wars, with guns such as Big Bertha and the German Schwerer Gustav, a railway gun of 80 cm calibre. Such guns took so long to move and deploy that they were vulnerable to air attack and unsuited to rapid warfare.
sierra-leone: Sierra Leone lies on the south-west coast of West Africa, bordered by Guinea to the north and east, Liberia to the south-east and the Atlantic Ocean to the west. It has about 400 km of coastline. The east is a plateau with high mountains, where Mount Bintumani reaches 1,948 m, and lowland plains of forest, bush and farmland cover about 43% of the land. Freetown stands on a mountainous coastal peninsula. The name comes from the Lion Mountains near Freetown, which the Portuguese explorer Pedro de Sintra named Serra Leoa, meaning lioness mountains, in 1462.

The area has been inhabited for at least 2,500 years. Iron technology was adopted by the 9th century and agriculture established on the coast by about 1000 CE. Dense rainforest and swamps, and the tsetse fly, whose disease killed the horses and zebu cattle of the Mandé people, protected the region against invasion by the Mandinka Empire and limited the influence of the Mali Empire. Susu traders brought Islam in the 18th century.

European contact began in the 15th century. Traders from the Dutch Republic, England and France set up stations that came to deal mainly in slaves, brought to the coast by traders from the interior. In 1808 the coastal Sierra Leone Colony was founded as part of the British Empire, to resettle Africans returning after the abolition of the slave trade, and in 1896 an inland Protectorate was created. Independence came in 1961 under Prime Minister Sir Milton Margai. A constitution of 1971 made the country a presidential republic under Siaka Stevens. In 1991 a civil war began between the government and the Revolutionary United Front. It lasted 11 years and ended in 2002 after intervention by ECOMOG forces and then the United Kingdom.

Freetown is the capital and largest city. The country is a presidential republic, and English is the official language, while Krio, derived from English and several African languages, is spoken across the country. About 18 ethnic groups live there, the Temne and Mende being the largest, and the Creole people descend from freed African-American and Afro-Caribbean slaves and liberated Africans. Bunce Island, near Freetown, holds the ruins of a slave fortress of the Atlantic slave trade.
sigmund-freud: Sigmund Freud was born Sigismund Schlomo Freud on 6 May 1856 in the Moravian town of Freiberg, in the Austrian Empire, now Příbor in the Czech Republic. He was the first of eight children of Ashkenazi Jewish parents who both came from Galicia. His father, Jakob Freud, was a wool merchant, and his mother, Amalia Nathansohn, was Jakob's third wife. The family was struggling financially and living in a rented room when he was born. He was born with a caul, which his mother saw as a good omen.

Freud took almost nine years to finish his medical studies, because of his interest in neurophysiological research, including the sexual anatomy of eels, and in philosophy under Franz Brentano. He entered private practice in neurology for financial reasons and received his doctorate in medicine in 1881, aged 25. In the 1880s he worked chiefly on the anatomy of the brain. In 1891 his monograph Zur Auffassung der Aphasien entered the debates about aphasia, coined the term agnosia and counselled against too locationist a view of neurological deficits.

He was also an early researcher of cerebral palsy, then called cerebral paralysis, and showed that the disease existed long before other researchers studied it. He suggested that William John Little, who first identified it, was wrong that lack of oxygen at birth was a cause, and proposed instead that birth complications were a symptom. Freud died on 23 September 1939.

Freud founded psychoanalysis, a clinical method that treats conflicts in the psyche through dialogue between patient and analyst. He introduced free association, the interpretation of dreams and the analysis of transference. He widened the idea of sexuality to include infantile stages, which led to the Oedipus complex, and developed a theory of the unconscious and a model of the mind with id, ego and superego. His later work offered an interpretation and critique of religion and culture.

His books include The Interpretation of Dreams (1899), Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality (1905), Totem and Taboo (1913), The Ego and the Id (1923), The Future of an Illusion (1927), Civilization and Its Discontents (1930) and Moses and Monotheism (1939). His talking cure gave the basic format for later psychotherapy. The neo-Freudians, among them Alfred Adler and Karen Horney, rejected his theory of instinctual drive, and Jacques Lacan approached psychoanalysis through linguistics and literature. His legacy remains controversial.
singapore: Singapore lies about one degree of latitude, 137 kilometres, north of the equator, off the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula. Its territory is a main island, also known as Pulau Ujong, over 60 satellite islands and one outlying islet, and two man-made connections, the Johor–Singapore Causeway and the Tuas Second Link, join it to Johor in Malaysia. The highest natural point is Bukit Timah Hill, at 163.63 metres. Land reclamation has raised the land area from roughly 580 km2 in the 1960s to 770 km2. The name is an anglicisation of the Malay Singapura, from the Sanskrit for 'lion city', and the island was earlier known as Temasek.

According to the Malay Annals, the Kingdom of Singapura was founded in 1299 by Sang Nila Utama, although historians debate the accounts. In the 14th century, as Temasek, Singapore was a trading port under the influence of both the Majapahit Empire and the Siamese kingdoms. Around the end of that century its ruler Parameswara was attacked, by either the Majapahit or the Siamese, and moved to Malacca, where he founded the Sultanate of Malacca. Portuguese raiders burned the settlement in 1613, and the island then faded into obscurity for two centuries, nominally part of the Johor Sultanate.

Stamford Raffles arrived on 28 January 1819, when around 150 people lived on the island, 120 of them Malays. With the help of the Temenggong of Johor, he brought Tengku Long back from exile and recognised him as Sultan Hussein, and in the Treaty of Singapore of 6 February 1819 the Sultan granted the British the right to establish a trading post. Singapore came under direct British control in 1867 as part of the Straits Settlements, was occupied by Japan in 1942, gained self-governance in 1959 and joined Malaysia in 1963. It was expelled from the federation two years later and became independent in 1965.

Singapore is a parliamentary republic based on the Westminster system. Its population was 6,110,200 in 2025, of whom 3,660,200 were citizens. The 2020 census reported 74.3% of residents of Chinese descent, 13.5% Malay and 9.0% Indian. English, Malay, Mandarin and Tamil are the four official languages, and 78.7% of resident households live in public housing developed by the Housing and Development Board.
slovakia: Slovakia covers about 49,000 km2 and is mostly mountainous, with the Carpathian Mountains across most of the northern half. The Tatra Mountains hold 29 peaks above 2,500 metres, and Gerlachovský štít, at 2,655 metres, is the highest point in the country. The largest lowland is the Danubian Lowland in the southwest, followed by the Eastern Slovak Lowland in the southeast. Forests cover 41% of the land, nine national parks cover 6.5%, and hundreds of caves lie under the mountains, five of them on UNESCO's World Heritage list. The name means the Land of the Slavs, and the present Slovak form Slovensko is first attested in 1675.

The oldest human artefacts, stone tools dated to 270,000 BCE, come from near Nové Mesto nad Váhom, and a Neanderthal cranium of about 200,000 BCE was found near Gánovce. Slavs arrived in the 5th and 6th centuries, and parts of the territory came under the Avar Khaganate before the Principality of Nitra was annexed by the Principality of Moravia, later Great Moravia. The land passed into the Principality of Hungary, which became the Kingdom of Hungary in 1000. The Mongol invasion of 1241 and 1242 destroyed much of it, and the south was part of Ottoman provinces in the 16th and 17th centuries.

The Slovak Uprising of 1848 did not achieve its aim but helped to cement a Slovak national identity. Czechoslovakia was proclaimed in 1918, with its borders set by the Treaty of Saint Germain in 1919 and the Treaty of Trianon in 1920. The first Slovak Republic, established in 1939 as a one-party clerical fascist client state under Nazi Germany, joined the Axis in 1940. Czechoslovakia became a communist state after the Soviet-backed coup of 1948, the Prague Spring was suppressed by the Warsaw Pact invasion in August 1968, and the Velvet Revolution of 1989 ended communist rule.

Slovakia became independent on 1 January 1993 after the peaceful dissolution of Czechoslovakia, and its constitution, ratified on 1 September 1992, took effect that day. It is a parliamentary democratic republic with a directly elected president of limited powers and a 150-seat National Council. It joined the European Union and NATO in 2004, the Schengen Area in 2007 and the eurozone in 2009.

The 2021 census recorded 83.8% Slovaks and 7.8% Hungarians, the largest minority, and 55.8% of the population identified as Catholic. About 90,000 Jews lived in Slovakia before the Second World War, and most were murdered in the Holocaust; about 2,300 remain.
slovenia: Slovenia covers 20,271 km2 and is mostly mountainous and forested. Four major European geographic regions meet there: the Alps, the Dinarides, the Pannonian Plain and the Mediterranean Sea. The highest peak, Triglav, at 2,864 metres, appears on the national coat of arms and flag. The Adriatic coastline stretches approximately 47 kilometres, the southwest has a limestone Karst Plateau of underground rivers, gorges and caves, and the landscape of the northeast is essentially flat. The name means land of the Slavs.

Evidence of habitation dates to around 250,000 years ago. A pierced cave bear bone from Divje Babe cave near Cerkno, dated to 43100 ± 700 years before present, is considered a kind of flute and possibly the oldest musical instrument discovered. Pile dwellings over 4,500 years old in the Ljubljana Marsh are a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the Ljubljana Marshes Wooden Wheel is the world's oldest wooden wheel. In Roman times the area was divided between Venetia et Histria and the provinces of Pannonia and Noricum, with posts at Emona (Ljubljana), Poetovio (Ptuj) and Celeia (Celje). In 394 the Battle of the Frigidus took place in the Vipava Valley, where Theodosius I defeated the usurper Eugenius.

Slavic tribes migrated to the Alpine area after the Lombards departed in 568. From 623 or 624 King Samo united the Alpine and Western Slavs against the Avars, and after his death around 658 the ancestors of the Slovenes formed Carantania and Carniola. Charlemagne decisively defeated the Avars in 803. The Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes was formed in December 1918 and became known as Yugoslavia in 1929. Nazi Germany, Fascist Italy, Hungary and the Independent State of Croatia partitioned Slovenia in 1941.

Slovenia was established in 1945 as one of six republics of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and modern Slovenia emerged in June 1991, when it declared independence and became a sovereign state after the brief Ten-Day War. It is a parliamentary republic whose head of state is a president elected for five years, and legislative power rests mainly with the 90-member National Assembly. In 2007 it was the first new member state of the European Union to adopt the euro. The population is about 2.1 million, and Slovenes make up 83.1% of the inhabitants. Four sites are on UNESCO's World Heritage list, among them the Škocjan Caves and the Idrija Mercury mining site.
socialist-party-of-albania: The Party of Labour of Albania, founded by Enver Hoxha, had ruled the country for over four decades. Hoxha's successor, Ramiz Alia, was forced to introduce limited reforms in the late 1980s, and on 11 December 1990 he announced that the party had given up its monopoly of power. It won the Constitutional Assembly election of 1991, the first free elections held in Albania in almost 80 years, by which time it was no longer a Marxist-Leninist party. At an extraordinary congress held from 10 to 13 June 1991 it reorganised itself as the Socialist Party in order to survive in the new system.

Fatos Nano, a man from the intelligentsia, was elected the first chairman. He helped to reform the old communist party and brought it into the Socialist International. In 2004 a faction led by Ilir Meta broke away and formed the Socialist Movement for Integration. On 10 October 2005, after losing the parliamentary election of that year, Nano resigned and was succeeded by Edi Rama.

Under Rama the party formed the Alliance for a European Albania, which united several parties and won the parliamentary election of 2013, returning the Socialists to government after eight years. Running alone, the party won the elections of 2017 and 2021 with 74 seats in each, enough to govern by itself, though it has had the outside support of the Social Democratic Party in parliament.

The party is described as social-democratic. Its platform of 2013 pledged to replace the flat tax with a progressive tax and supported universal health care. It is pro-European, supports Albania's accession to the European Union and its membership of NATO, and regards Kosovo as the country's main strategic partner and ally. It is an associate of the Party of European Socialists. Its emblem is based on the fist and rose designed by José María Cruz Novillo for the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party in 1977, used without that party's official consent.
socrates: Socrates left no writings, and what is known of him comes from others: his pupils Plato and Xenophon, the comic dramatist Aristophanes, and Aristotle, who was born after his death. These accounts often contradict one another, a difficulty scholars call the Socratic problem. Xenophon wrote about him in the Memorabilia, the Oeconomicus, the Symposium and the Apology. How far Plato's dialogues portray the historical Socrates is debated, and some scholars distinguish an earlier, more faithful portrait from a later one carrying Plato's own views.

Socrates was born in 470 or 469 BCE in the Athenian deme of Alopece, to Sophroniscus, a stoneworker, and Phaenarete, a midwife. He had the usual education of a well-off Athenian and served in three campaigns of the Peloponnesian War, according to Plato. He married Xanthippe, with whom he had three sons, and also a daughter of the statesman Aristides. He was indifferent to comfort, owned one ragged coat and walked barefoot, and he criticised both the democrats and the oligarchs of Athens.

The method named for him, the elenchus, is shown mainly in Plato's early dialogues. Socrates asks an apparent expert for a definition, and further questions lead the expert to contradict it. A new definition is then tested in the same way. The discussion usually ends in an impasse, with the interlocutor unable to define what he thought he understood. Socrates frequently proclaimed his ignorance, saying he was sure only that he did not know.

Scholars dispute what the method achieves. In 1982 Gregory Vlastos argued that it could show only that an interlocutor's beliefs were inconsistent. Because Socrates taught no fixed doctrine, later schools drew different conclusions.

In 399 BCE Socrates was accused of impiety and of corrupting the youth. The accusation was brought by a poet, Meletus, with Anytus and Lycon. The trial came after the defeat of Athens by Sparta at the Battle of Aegospotami in 404 BCE and the rule of the Thirty Tyrants, and it probably lasted most of a day. A jury of hundreds of citizens found him guilty. He proposed free meals from the state, or alternatively a fine of one mina of silver, and the jurors ordered his death. Plato relates that he was put to death with hemlock after refusing offers to help him escape.

Almost every philosophical current after Socrates traced its roots to him, among them Plato's Academy, Aristotle's Lyceum, the Cynics and the Stoics, except the Epicureans and the Pyrrhonists. He was considered to have shifted philosophy from the natural world to human affairs.
somalia: Somalia is the easternmost country in continental Africa. It borders Ethiopia, Djibouti and Kenya, and has the longest coastline on the mainland, more than 3,333 kilometres, along the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. Its land area is 637,657 square kilometres of plateaus, plains and highlands. In the north a semi-desert plain, the Guban, runs parallel to the Gulf of Aden coast, and the Cal Madow range contains the highest peak, Shimbiris, at about 2,416 metres. The country sits at the mouth of the Bab el Mandeb gateway to the Red Sea.

The oldest evidence of burial customs in the Horn of Africa comes from cemeteries in Somalia dating to the 4th millennium BCE. The Laas Geel rock art near Hargeisa is approximately 5,000 years old. Ancient stone ruins have been taken as evidence of a civilisation that traded with Egypt and Mycenaean Greece from the second millennium BCE, supporting the hypothesis that Somalia or adjacent regions were the Land of Punt. An Egyptian expedition to Punt sent by Queen Hatshepsut is recorded on the reliefs at Deir el-Bahari. Puntites traded myrrh, spices, gold, ebony, ivory and frankincense.

In the Middle Ages the Ajuran Sultanate, Adal Sultanate and Sultanate of the Geledi dominated regional trade. The Italian and British empires colonised the sultanates in the late 19th century, forming Italian Somaliland and British Somaliland, which united in 1960 as the Somali Republic. Siad Barre seized power in 1969, launched a failed invasion of Ethiopia and brutally attempted to quash the Somaliland War of Independence.

Barre's regime collapsed in 1991 with the onset of the Somali Civil War. A provisional constitution adopted on 1 August 2012 made Somalia a federation. About 85 per cent of residents are ethnic Somalis. Somali is the official language, Arabic is recognised as a second, and the overwhelming majority are Sunni Muslims. About 80 per cent of the population are nomadic or semi-nomadic pastoralists.
sonderbund-war: In the early 1840s the radical Free Democratic Party of Switzerland, strong in the largely Protestant cantons and among the urban bourgeoisie, won a majority in the Federal Diet, the Tagsatzung, and proposed a new constitution that would draw the cantons closer together. The Diet had also acted against the Catholic Church, closing the monasteries and convents of Aargau in 1841 and seizing their property. When Lucerne recalled the Jesuits to head its education, bands of armed radicals known as Freischärler invaded the canton.

In 1845 Lucerne, Fribourg, Valais, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden and Zug, all predominantly Catholic and under conservative governments, formed the Sonderbund, or separate alliance. Ticino and Solothurn, Catholic but liberal, stayed out. On 21 October 1847 the Diet ordered the league dissolved as a breach of the Federal Treaty of 1815, which forbade such alliances. Austria sent the Sonderbund some money and munitions, but the great powers could not agree on intervention, which Lord Palmerston of Britain refused to support.

The Sonderbund's commander was Jean-Ulrich de Salis-Soglio of Grisons, himself a Protestant. The Diet's choice, Guillaume Henri Dufour of Geneva, was sworn in on 25 October after first declining the office. Neuchâtel and Appenzell Innerrhoden declared themselves neutral and sent no troops. The Sonderbund moved first: troops from Uri seized the St. Gotthard Pass in early November, and the first deaths came on 4 November.

Dufour turned first on isolated Fribourg, which surrendered on 14 November; its act of surrender became the template for the other cantons. Zug's parliament voted to give up on 21 November. On 23 November the federal divisions converged on Lucerne. At Gisikon a third assault, led in person by Colonel Eduard Ziegler, carried the Sonderbund position after two hours; thirty-seven men were killed and about 100 wounded. Federal troops entered Lucerne unopposed the next morning. Unterwalden, Schwyz and Uri yielded between 25 and 27 November, and Valais on 29 November.

The federal army reported 78 killed and 260 wounded; later research arrived at 60 dead and 386 wounded on the federal side and 33 killed and 124 wounded among the Sonderbund. Dufour had ordered his troops to care for the injured and declined to use Congreve rockets, so as not to give the war a violent character. The Sonderbund governments were forced to resign, and Liberals took power in Fribourg, Lucerne and Valais. Federal troops left the occupied cantons by February 1848. The constitution of that year banished the Jesuits from Switzerland, a provision lifted by a vote on 20 May 1973.
south-africa: South Africa covers 1,221,037 square kilometres at the southern tip of Africa, with 2,798 kilometres of coastline along the South Atlantic and Indian oceans, and it encloses Lesotho. The interior is a large, almost flat plateau between 1,000 and 2,100 metres high, surrounded by the Great Escarpment, whose eastern stretch is the Drakensberg; Mafadi, at 3,450 metres, is the highest peak. The south-western plateau is the sparsely populated Great Karoo, and the well-watered Highveld holds a great proportion of the commercial farmland and the largest conurbation, Gauteng. The country has three capitals: Pretoria, Cape Town and Bloemfontein.

South Africa holds some of the oldest archaeological and human-fossil sites in the world, among them the caves of the Cradle of Humankind in Gauteng, and modern humans have inhabited Southern Africa for at least 170,000 years. The indigenous San and Khoikhoi were predominantly hunter-gatherers, and the Khoikhoi also practised pastoralism; they were largely displaced or absorbed by the Bantu expansion between 1,500 and 2,000 years ago.

The Kingdom of Mapungubwe formed in the north in the 13th century, and the Venda Kingdom in the 17th. The Dutch established the first European settlement at Table Bay in 1652, the Cape Colony. Its invasion in 1795 and the Battle of Blaauwberg in 1806 led to British occupation, and the Mfecane, a period of upheaval, led to the formation of kingdoms including the Zulu Kingdom.

The Mineral Revolution brought industrialisation and urbanisation. After the Second Boer War the Union of South Africa was created in 1910 by the amalgamation of the Cape, Natal, Transvaal and Orange River colonies, and it became a republic after the 1961 referendum. The multi-racial Cape Qualified Franchise was gradually eroded, and the vast majority of black South Africans were not enfranchised until 1994. The National Party imposed apartheid in 1948, institutionalising earlier racial segregation, and after a struggle by the African National Congress and others the repeal of discriminatory laws began in the mid-1980s.

Universal elections took place in 1994, and since then all racial groups have held political representation in a parliamentary republic of nine provinces, in which the president is both head of state and head of government. The 2022 census counted Black African South Africans at 81%, Coloured at 8.2%, White at 7.3% and Indian or Asian at 2.7%. The country has 12 official languages and has been called the rainbow nation.
south-america: South America lies entirely in the Western Hemisphere and mostly in the Southern Hemisphere. It is bordered on the west by the Pacific Ocean, on the north and east by the Atlantic Ocean, and on the south by the Drake Passage, and it has an area of 17,840,000 square kilometres. The geography of the west is dominated by the Andes, the longest mountain range in the world, whose highest mountain is Aconcagua at 6,962 metres. The east contains highlands and vast lowlands where the Amazon, Orinoco and Paraná flow.

The continent holds several superlatives: Angel Falls in Venezuela is the world's highest uninterrupted waterfall, the Amazon is the largest river by volume, and the Atacama Desert is the driest non-polar place on earth. Lake Titicaca is the highest commercially navigable lake. Most of the population lives near the western or eastern coasts, forming what is called a hollow continent.

South America is thought to have been first inhabited by people who crossed the Bering Land Bridge at least 15,000 years ago and moved south through North America. The Monte Verde II site in Chile, suggested to date to around 14,500 years ago, is among the oldest evidence of human presence. Ancient DNA evidence shows that the peopling was more complex than a single migration, with at least three major dispersals. Llamas and alpacas were domesticated in the Andean highlands circa 3500 BCE.

Caral-Supe on the central Peruvian coast, generally dated to around 3500 BCE, was a pre-ceramic culture whose monumental architecture created one of the first cities of the world. Chavín followed by 900 BCE according to some estimates, and its civilisation spanned 900 to 300 BCE, with artefacts found at Chavín de Huántar in Peru. Irrigation systems and widespread fishing helped establish agrarian societies by 2000 BCE.

The continent includes twelve sovereign countries, two dependent territories and one internal territory, French Guiana. Brazil covers a little less than half of its land area and holds around half of its population. Most countries are presidential republics, and Guyana and Suriname are parliamentary republics. It is the only inhabited continent without monarchies, though the Empire of Brazil existed in the 19th century.

The population is estimated at more than 434 million. Spanish and Portuguese are by far the most spoken languages, with approximately 200 million speakers each. Indigenous languages include Quechua, Aymara and Guaraní, which are recognised with Spanish as national languages.
south-korea: The Korean Peninsula was inhabited as early as the Lower Paleolithic. According to Korea's founding mythology, the history of Korea begins with the founding of Gojoseon in 2333 BCE by Dangun; Chinese records note Gojoseon in the early 7th century BCE. In 108 BCE the Han dynasty defeated Wiman Joseon and installed four commanderies in the north of the peninsula. The Lelang commandery remained a centre of cultural and economic exchange for four centuries, until Goguryeo conquered it in 313 CE.

From the Proto-Three Kingdoms states of Buyeo, Okjeo, Dongye and Samhan emerged the Three Kingdoms of Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla. Goguryeo was the largest and a highly militaristic state, with 700 years of history. Under Gwanggaeto the Great and his son Jangsu it subdued Baekje and Silla. In the Goguryeo-Sui War it is said to have defeated a force of over a million men.

The Goryeo dynasty (918 to 1392) achieved lasting unification, and the Joseon dynasty (1392 to 1897) followed it, maintaining an isolationist policy from the mid-17th century. The Korean Empire (1897 to 1910) was annexed by the Empire of Japan in 1910. After Japan's surrender in World War II, Korea was divided into a Soviet-occupied northern zone and a United States-occupied southern zone, and the Republic of Korea was established in August 1948.

The Korean War began in 1950 with a North Korean invasion and ended in 1953 with an armistice, with three million Koreans dead and both economies in ruins. No peace treaty was signed. South Korea then endured a series of dictatorships punctuated by coups, revolutions and violent uprisings, while its economy grew rapidly and it became one of the Four Asian Tigers. The June Democratic Struggle of 1987 ended authoritarian rule and led to the Sixth Republic.

Under the 1987 constitution South Korea is a unitary presidential republic with a unicameral National Assembly. It is divided into ten provinces, three special self-governing provinces and several cities with special status. Its recorded economic growth was among the fastest between the early 1960s and the late 1990s; South Koreans call this the Miracle on the Han River.

The population was roughly 51.7 million in 2022. South Korea shares its traditional culture with North Korea, though the two have developed distinct contemporary cultures since 1945. It has 16 World Heritage Sites.
south-sudan: South Sudan lies between latitudes 3° and 13°N and is covered in tropical forest, swamps and grassland. The Nile river system runs south to north across its centre. The White Nile, known locally as the Bahr al Jabal, passes Juba and forms the Sudd, a large swamp of seasonally flooded grassland. Habitats include plateaus, savannahs, floodplains and wetlands, and Bandingilo National Park hosts one of the largest wildlife migrations in the world.

The Nilotic peoples of the region, among them the Dinka, Anyuak, Bari, Acholi, Nuer and Shilluk, first entered South Sudan sometime before the tenth century. From the 15th to the 19th century migrations, largely from the area of Bahr el Ghazal, brought the Anyuak, Dinka, Nuer and Shilluk to their modern locations, while the Acholi and Bari settled in Equatoria. The Zande and others, who entered in the 16th century, established the region's largest state, in Equatoria. In the 18th century the Avungara sib rose to power over the rest of Azande society.

Egypt under Khedive Ismail Pasha first tried to control the region in the 1870s, setting up the province of Equatoria; its governors were Samuel Baker from 1869, Charles George Gordon from 1874 and Emin Pasha from 1878. Sudan was governed as an Anglo-Egyptian condominium from 1899 until independence in 1956. British policies favouring Christian missionaries, such as the Closed District Ordinance of 1922, together with the swamplands along the White Nile, limited the spread of Islam to the south. Colonial policy emphasised the development of the Arabised north and largely ignored the south, which lacked schools, hospitals, roads and bridges.

After Sudan's first independent elections in 1958, continued neglect of the south by the Khartoum government led to revolts and the longest civil war on the continent. Following the First Sudanese Civil War the Southern Sudan Autonomous Region was formed in 1972 and lasted until 1983, when the Second Sudanese Civil War began. It ended with the Comprehensive Peace Agreement of 2005, and southern autonomy was restored. More than 2 million people are said to have died in the wars and more than 4 million were displaced. South Sudan became independent on 9 July 2011 after 98.8% voted for independence in a referendum in January 2011.

South Sudan is a landlocked country in East Africa, and its capital and largest city is Juba. Its transitional constitution, in force since 9 July 2011, sets up a presidential system with a two-house National Legislature. The population is composed mostly of Nilotic peoples, the Dinka being the largest group, followed by the Nuer and the Azande. The common languages are Juba Arabic and English. A civil war was fought from 2013 to 2018.
soviet-union: The word soviet means council in Russian. Soviets as workers' councils first appeared during the 1905 Russian Revolution and were quickly suppressed. After the February Revolution of 1917, workers' and soldiers' soviets emerged across the country and shared power with the Russian Provisional Government. The Bolsheviks, led by Vladimir Lenin, demanded that all power pass to the soviets, and after the October Revolution they seized power in their name. Following the Bolshevik victory in the Russian Civil War, the Russian Socialist Federal Soviet Republic and its subordinate republics were merged into the Soviet Union in 1922.

War communism involved nationalisation of industry and forced requisition of agricultural production. After a severe economic collapse Lenin replaced it in 1921 with the New Economic Policy, which legalised free trade and private ownership of small businesses. After Lenin's death in 1924 Joseph Stalin emerged as undisputed ruler. By 1928–1929 he had abandoned the New Economic Policy for full central planning, forced collectivisation and rapid industrialisation. Collectivisation is linked to a devastating famine in the 1930s that killed millions. The Gulag was expanded, and the Great Purge of the late 1930s brought deportations, executions and the Moscow trials.

The Soviet Union signed a non-aggression pact with Nazi Germany in 1939, and Germany invaded in 1941. The Soviet Union suffered around 27 million casualties, the most deaths of any country in the Second World War. The Cold War followed, and Soviet forces suppressed uprisings in East Germany, Hungary and Czechoslovakia. Mikhail Gorbachev sought reform from 1985 through glasnost and perestroika. After a failed coup by hardliners in 1991, Russia, Ukraine and Belarus seceded, and on 26 December Gorbachev recognised the dissolution of the Soviet Union. All fifteen republics became independent.

The Soviet Union was a federal union of national republics, the largest being the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic. The Communist Party governed under Marxism–Leninism through soviet councils, and the general secretary of the party's Central Committee was the de facto highest office. Elections were uncontested. The economy was centrally planned. Its area of 22,402,200 square kilometres made it the world's largest country, with its capital and largest city at Moscow. Culture went through stages: relative freedom of artistic experiment in the first decade, then under Stalin the imposed style of socialist realism, with other trends severely repressed and many writers imprisoned or killed.
spain: Spain covers most of the Iberian Peninsula and has an area of 505,992 square kilometres, making it Europe's fourth largest country. It also includes the Balearic Islands in the Mediterranean, the Canary Islands in the Atlantic and the autonomous cities of Ceuta and Melilla in North Africa, so that it is a transcontinental country. Mount Teide on Tenerife, at 3,715 metres, is the highest peak in Spain. The Pyrenees form the border with France and Andorra, and the border with Portugal, at 1,214 kilometres, is the longest uninterrupted border within the European Union.
