Archaeological research at Atapuerca shows that the Iberian Peninsula was populated by hominids very early, and Neanderthal populations survived in parts of Iberia until around 40,000 years ago. The paintings in the Altamira cave of Cantabria were created from 35,600 to 13,500 BCE. Before the Roman conquest the major cultures were the Iberians along the Mediterranean coast, the Celts in the interior and north-west, the Lusitanians in the west and the Tartessians in the southwest, while Phoenicians, Carthaginians and Greeks established trading settlements. The Roman conquest created the province of Hispania. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire the Visigoths established a kingdom centred on Toledo.

In the early 8th century the Umayyad Caliphate conquered most of the peninsula, with Al-Andalus centred on Córdoba. The northern Christian kingdoms launched the so-called Reconquista, which culminated with the fall of the Nasrid Kingdom of Granada.

The union of the Crown of Castile and the Crown of Aragon in 1479 under the Catholic Monarchs is often seen as the de facto unification of Spain as a nation state. During the Age of Discovery Spain led the exploration and conquest of the New World, completed the first circumnavigation of the globe and established one of the largest empires in history. The 19th century brought the Peninsular War of 1808 to 1814 and the loss of most American colonies, and the Spanish Civil War of 1936 to 1939 was followed by the Francoist dictatorship until 1975.

Spain had a population of 49,570,725 in 2026, with Madrid as the capital and largest city. A national referendum on 6 December 1978 approved the new constitution with 88% of voters, and Spain transitioned from a one-party personalist dictatorship to a multiparty parliamentary democracy of seventeen autonomous communities and two autonomous cities. It is a parliamentary monarchy with King Felipe VI as head of state. Spain joined the European Economic Community in 1986 and took part in the launch of the euro in 1999.
spanish-language: Spanish evolved from the Vulgar Latin that the Romans brought to the Iberian Peninsula during the Second Punic War, beginning in 210 BCE. Several pre-Roman languages had been spoken there, including Proto-Basque, Iberian, Lusitanian, Celtiberian and Gallaecian. The first documents to show traces of what is regarded as the precursor of modern Spanish date from the 9th century, and the first systematic written use of the language happened in Toledo in the 13th century.

The language takes its alternative name, castellano, from the Kingdom of Castile. The Spanish Constitution of 1978 uses castellano for the official language of the whole of Spain. The Royal Spanish Academy, founded in 1713, called the language castellano from 1713 to 1923 and now prefers español, though it regards both terms as synonymous and equally valid.

Spanish is a fusional Romance language of the Ibero-Romance group, written in the Latin script with the addition of the letter ñ. It has five vowel phonemes and between 17 and 19 consonant phonemes, depending on the dialect. Nouns and adjectives have two genders and two numbers, and there are about fifty conjugated forms per verb. About 75% of the modern vocabulary is Latin in origin.

Other influences on the vocabulary came from neighbouring Romance languages such as Mozarabic, Catalan, Portuguese and Occitan, and from Andalusi Arabic, with about 8% of the vocabulary having Arabic roots. Words from Quechua, Nahuatl and other indigenous languages of the Americas were also absorbed, and French, English and German loanwords arrived in the 18th to 20th centuries. For written Portuguese and Spanish, Ethnologue gives a lexical similarity of 89%.

Spanish colonialism in the early modern period carried the language overseas, most notably to the Americas. It is now the world's second-most spoken native language, with an estimated 519 million native speakers in 2025 and about 636 million speakers in total. Mexico has the largest population of native speakers, with about 130 million.

Spanish is an official language of the United Nations and the European Union. The Association of Spanish Language Academies, created in Mexico in 1951, unites the academies of 23 countries. In the United States, Spanish is the second most spoken language, and over 50 million people were estimated to speak it in 2015.
sri-lanka: Sri Lanka lies in the Indian Ocean between latitudes 5° and 10° N, separated from the Indian subcontinent by the Gulf of Mannar and the Palk Strait. According to Hindu mythology a land bridge once joined the island to India. It now amounts to a chain of limestone shoals, and legends claim it was passable on foot until 1480 CE, when cyclones deepened the channel. The island consists mostly of flat to rolling coastal plains, with mountains rising only in the south-central part. The highest point is Pidurutalagala at 2,524 metres, and the longest river is the Mahaweli, at 335 kilometres. The coastline is 1,585 kilometres long.

Prehistory on the island goes back 125,000 years and possibly 500,000. In caves such as Pahiyangala, Batadombalena and Belilena archaeologists found the remains of anatomically modern humans, named Balangoda Man. The earliest inhabitants were likely ancestors of the Vedda people. During the protohistoric period, 1000 to 500 BCE, the island was culturally united with southern India and shared its megalithic burials, pottery, iron technology and farming techniques.

According to the Mahāvaṃsa, a Pāḷi chronicle written in the 5th century CE, the original inhabitants were the Yakshas and Nagas, and Sinhalese history traditionally begins in 543 BCE with the arrival of the semi-historical Prince Vijaya, who sailed with 700 followers after being expelled from Vanga, present-day Bengal. Vijaya is the first of about 189 monarchs described in chronicles such as the Dīpavaṃsa, Mahāvaṃsa and Cūḷavaṃsa.

The earliest known Buddhist writings on the island, the Pali Canon, date back to 29 BCE. The island was known to explorers as early as the Anuradhapura period. The Portuguese reached it in 1505 and established a colony in the sixteenth century, the Dutch later controlled the coastal areas, and the British established a colony by the early 19th century. Independence came in 1948 as the Dominion of Ceylon, and the country became a republic in 1972. A civil war between Tamil separatists and the armed forces lasted from 1983 to 2009.

Colombo is the executive and judicial capital and the largest city, and Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte is the legislative capital. The island has been called by many names: Taprobanā by Greek geographers, Sarandīb by Arabs and Persians, and Ceilão by the Portuguese, which became Ceylon in English. Sinhala and Tamil are the official languages. The Sinhalese form about 74% of the population and Sri Lankan Tamils about 12%, with Moors, Indian Tamils, Burghers, Malays and Veddas among smaller communities. Buddhism is the largest religion, and Sinhalese culture, centred in Kandy and Anuradhapura, and Tamil culture, centred in Jaffna, are the two main traditions.
state-protection-authority: The force began in 1945 as the Budapest Department of State Political Police. In 1946 it became the State Defence Department of the Hungarian State Police, the ÁVO, and in 1950 the State Protection Authority. Gábor Péter headed it from 1945 to 1952. László Rajk, the Communist minister of the interior, played a crucial part in organising it, and in 1949 became one of its victims: he was arrested, tried for nationalism and Titoism and executed. On 1 January 1950 the authority was removed from the Ministry of the Interior, made independent and given the Border Guard.

The authority served the Hungarian Working People's Party directly, with little reference to the norms of government, and its actions were not subject to judicial review until the early years after Stalin. It gathered intelligence through a vast network of informants. Secret arrests were followed by periods of torture lasting from 3 to 18 months, after which the public prosecutors and courts were called in to pass sentence.

Prisons and internment camps were placed under its supervision, the most notorious at Recsk, Kistarcsa, Tiszalök and Kazincbarcika. Before 1953 some camps aimed at the eventual death of their inmates through overwork and maltreatment. The first government of Imre Nagy, from 1953 to 1955, greatly improved conditions in the camps and ended these efforts.

In 1953 the authority prepared a show trial meant to prove that Raoul Wallenberg had not been taken to the Soviet Union in 1945 but had been killed by Zionists in Budapest. Leaders of the Jewish community, among them Miksa Domonkos and Lajos Stöckler, and two intended witnesses were seized and tortured. After the death of Stalin the preparations were stopped and the prisoners released in the autumn of 1953. Domonkos died shortly afterwards, mainly from the torture.

On 29 October 1956, during the revolution, the militia of József Dudás stormed the secret police headquarters and massacred the officers inside, and the crowd lynched others. The students' and workers' councils then set up armed patrols to detain members of the authority for their own safety and for later trial. When Soviet forces intervened, its officers carried out brutal reprisals against revolutionaries.

The government of János Kádár, who had himself been tortured by the authority, did not revive it under its old name. Its work passed to a department of the Ministry of the Interior, known as III, which operated with considerably more restraint. Its former headquarters at 60 Andrássy Avenue in Budapest is now a museum, the House of Terror.
stockholm: Stockholm lies on Sweden's east coast at the 59th parallel north, where the freshwater Lake Mälaren flows out into the Baltic Sea. The central parts of the city consist of fourteen islands that continue into the Stockholm archipelago. More than 30% of the city area is waterways and another 30% parks and green spaces. Its position, at the eastern end of the Central Swedish lowland and near the Bergslagen region, reflects the early orientation of Swedish trade toward the Baltic.

The area was settled from the Stone Age, in the 6th millennium BCE. Norse sagas name the location as Agnafit, and Birka, near Stockholm, was one of Sweden's major trade centres in the Viking Age. Numerous runestones were carved in the area because of its importance as a trading hub.

The earliest written mention of the name Stockholm dates from 1252, by which time the mines of Bergslagen had made it an important site in the iron trade. Stock means log in Swedish, though it may also connect to an old German word meaning fortification, and holm means islet, probably the islet of Helgeandsholmen. According to Erik's Chronicle the city was founded by Birger Jarl to protect Sweden from sea invasions by Karelians, after the pillage of Sigtuna on Lake Mälaren in the summer of 1187.

The Old Town, Gamla Stan, was built on the central island next to Helgeandsholmen from the mid-13th century onward. The city rose to prominence through the Baltic trade of the Hanseatic League, developing strong economic and cultural links with Lübeck, Hamburg, Gdańsk, Visby, Tallinn and Riga. Research and higher education in the sciences began in the 18th century. Karolinska Institutet was formalised in 1811 and KTH Royal Institute of Technology was founded in 1827. The city hosted the 1912 Summer Olympics, and the Stockholm Metro opened in 1950.

Stockholm is the capital and most populous city of Sweden. Its municipality had 984,748 inhabitants in 2022, with about 1.6 million in the urban area. It is the seat of the government and the Riksdag, and Stockholm Palace is the official residence of the Swedish monarch. The Vasa Museum is the most visited museum in Scandinavia. The Stockholm region has three World Heritage Sites: Drottningholm Palace, Skogskyrkogården and Birka. The Nobel Prize ceremonies and banquet are held in the city each year.
stuart-restoration: Richard Cromwell, Lord Protector from 1658 to 1659, ceded power to the Rump Parliament, and for a year government was dominated by the army leaders Charles Fleetwood and John Lambert. On 20 October 1659 George Monck, governor of Scotland under the Cromwells, marched south to oppose them. Lambert's army melted away and Monck reached London unopposed. The Presbyterian members excluded in Pride's Purge of 1648 were recalled, and on 24 December the Long Parliament was restored.

On 4 April 1660 Charles issued the Declaration of Breda, setting out his promises on recovering the crown. Monck organised the Convention Parliament, which first met on 25 April and on 8 May proclaimed that Charles II had been lawful king since the execution of Charles I on 30 January 1649. Charles left The Hague on 23 May, landed at Dover on 25 May and entered London on 29 May, his thirtieth birthday, a date kept afterwards as the holiday of Oak Apple Day. He was crowned at Westminster Abbey on 23 April 1661.

The Indemnity and Oblivion Act, law from 29 August 1660, pardoned past treason but excluded those involved in the trial and execution of Charles I. In October 1660 ten men were hanged, drawn and quartered in London, among them Thomas Harrison and the preacher Hugh Peters; three more followed on 19 April 1662, and a further 19 were imprisoned for life. In January 1661 the corpses of Oliver Cromwell, Henry Ireton and John Bradshaw were exhumed and hanged in chains at Tyburn.

The Cavalier Parliament, overwhelmingly royalist, met on 8 May 1661 and sat until 24 January 1679. The leading minister of the first years was Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon, and the Church of England was restored as the national church, backed by the Clarendon Code and the Act of Uniformity 1662. In Scotland the Rescissory Act 1661 annulled all legislation back to 1633; in Ireland the union of the Commonwealth years was treated as void, and James Butler, 1st Duke of Ormond, returned as Lord Lieutenant in 1662.

The colonies followed at different speeds. Barbados declared for the king in July 1660, Rhode Island in October 1660 and Massachusetts last, in August 1661; New Haven, which sheltered three regicides, was merged into Connecticut in 1662. The period is commonly taken to end with the Glorious Revolution of 1688, when William of Orange landed on 5 November and James II fled to France, and with the Bill of Rights 1689.
sudan: The modern state of Sudan covers 1,886,068 km2, the third-largest country in Africa by area, with an 853 km coast on the Red Sea. The terrain is generally flat plains broken by mountain ranges, and the highest point is the Deriba Caldera, at 3,042 metres, in the Marrah Mountains. The Blue Nile and White Nile meet at Khartoum to form the Nile, which flows north through Egypt.

The north and centre are extremely dry, with the Nubian and Bayuda deserts, while the south has grasslands and tropical savanna. The name comes from the Arabic bilad as-sudan, the Land of the Blacks, which was historically applied to the Sahel from Senegal to Northeast Africa; before that the area was known as Nubia.

The oldest evidence is the camp remains at Affad 23, some 50,000 years old, and the war of Jebel Sahaba, around 11500 BCE, is described as the earliest known war in the world. The Kingdom of Kerma flourished from about 2500 to 1500 BCE and in its last phase became a populous empire rivalling Egypt. Egyptian rulers of the New Kingdom then held the region, beginning when Thutmose I occupied Kush and destroyed Kerma. The Kingdom of Kush lasted from about 785 BCE to 350 CE, and after its fall the Nubians formed the Christian kingdoms of Nobatia, Makuria and Alodia.

Arab nomads settled most of Sudan between the 14th and 15th centuries. From the 16th to the 19th centuries the Funj sultanate dominated the centre and east, while Darfur ruled the west and the Ottomans the east. Egypt conquered the whole country in the 19th century. After the Mahdist Uprising was defeated by a joint Egyptian-British force, Egypt agreed in 1899 under British pressure to share sovereignty with the United Kingdom, and Sudan was in effect governed as a British possession. It became independent on 1 January 1956.

Sudan has known repeated civil war. The first, from 1955 to 1972, was followed by a second between government forces and southern rebels, which led to the independence of South Sudan in 2011. Sharia law applied from 1983 until 2020, when Sudan became a secular state.
suniti-devi: Suniti Devi was born on 30 September 1864, a daughter of Keshub Chandra Sen of Calcutta and Jagonmohini Sen. She was fourteen when she married. For two years afterwards she stayed in her father's house, since her husband left for London for higher studies immediately after the wedding. She had four sons and three daughters. Two of her sons, Rajendra Narayan and Jitendra Narayan, later became Maharajas of Cooch Behar. Her daughters Sudhira and Pratibha married the brothers Alan and Miles Mander of Wightwick Manor in England, and Sukriti married Jyotsna Nath Ghoshal, a nephew of Rabindranath Tagore.

In 1887, when she attended the Golden Jubilee of Queen Victoria with her husband, she was made a Companion of the Order of the Crown of India, the first Indian woman to receive the honour. She was also present at the Delhi Durbar of 1911.

The girls' school that her husband set up in her name in 1881, later called Suniti Academy, was her idea. She gave it annual grants, exempted the pupils from tuition fees and rewarded those who did well. She arranged for palace cars to carry the girls between home and school and, to avoid controversy, ordered the car windows to be curtained. With her sister Sucharu Devi, Maharani of Mayurbhanj, she financed the foundation of the Maharani Girls' High School in Darjeeling in 1908. She was President of the State Council and in 1932 the first President of the All Bengal Women's Union.

She was also an author. Bengal Dacoits and Tigers, a collection of short stories, was published in Calcutta in 1916. The Beautiful Mogul Princesses, published in London in 1918, tells the lives of Mumtaz Mahal, Zebunissa, Nur Jahan and another princess. The Autobiography of an Indian Princess appeared in London in 1921, and her last book, The Life of Princess Yashodara: Wife and Disciple of the Lord Buddha, in 1929. She died suddenly at Ranchi on 10 November 1932. In Cooch Behar the school, Sunity Road and a tank known as the Sunity Tank or Bairagi Dighi are named after her.
suriname: Suriname lies on the Guiana Shield on the northern coast of South America, bordered by the Atlantic Ocean to the north, French Guiana to the east, Brazil to the south and Guyana to the west. It is the smallest sovereign country in South America. The northern lowland coast has been cultivated, and most of the people live there. The south is tropical rainforest and sparsely inhabited savanna, covering about 80% of the land. The name may come from an Indigenous people called the Surinen, who lived there at the time of European contact. British settlers wrote it Surinam, which long remained the standard English spelling until the official change to Suriname in January 1978.

Indigenous settlement dates back to about 3,000 BCE. The Lokono were a nomadic coastal people who lived by hunting, foraging and fishing, and the Carib, using superior sailing ships, conquered them. British settlers founded the first European colony at Marshall's Creek on the Suriname River in 1630. Jews, expelled from Spain and Portugal, began to settle from the early 17th century and were granted freedom of religion in 1665. In 1667, in the negotiations leading to the Treaty of Breda, the Dutch kept the plantation colony they had gained from the English, and the English kept New Amsterdam, which they renamed New York.

Under Dutch rule Suriname was a lucrative plantation colony, mostly of sugar, driven by African slave labour. About 300,000 enslaved Africans were taken there from the mid-1600s to the early 1800s. After slavery was abolished in 1863, indentured servants were recruited mostly from British India and the Dutch East Indies. Suriname became a constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in 1954 and independent on 25 November 1975.

Suriname is a representative democratic republic under the Constitution of 1987. Paramaribo is the capital and largest city, home to nearly half the population. Dutch is the official language, and Sranan Tongo, an English-based creole, is widely used. No ethnic group forms a majority. The population includes descendants of indentured workers from India, Java and China and of enslaved Africans, among them the Maroons, whose ancestors escaped to the interior. The Central Suriname Nature Reserve, established in 1998, became a World Heritage Site in 2000.
sweden: Sweden lies on the eastern part of the Scandinavian Peninsula, west of the Baltic Sea and Gulf of Bothnia, and covers 450,295 square kilometres, making it the largest Nordic country. The Scandinavian mountain chain separates it from Norway, and Kebnekaise, at 2,096.8 metres, is the highest point. About 15% of the country lies north of the Arctic Circle, and around 65% of the land is forested. The north, Norrland, takes up almost 60% of the territory and is sparsely populated, while the highest density is in the Mälaren valley and around Stockholm. Vänern is the third largest lake in Europe.

Sweden's prehistory begins around 12,000 BCE, with reindeer-hunting camps of the Bromme culture in Scania. The Roman historian Tacitus first described the Swedes, as the Suiones, in his Germania of 98 CE, noting ships with a prow at each end. The runic script was in use among the south Scandinavian elite by at least the second century CE.

In the sixth century the Byzantine historian Jordanes named two tribes in Scandza now taken to be Swedes, the Suetidi and Suehans, who supplied black fox skins to the Roman world. The inhabitants emerged as the Geats and Swedes, part of the sea-faring Norsemen, and a unified Swedish state was established during the late 10th century.

In 1397 Sweden joined Norway and Denmark in the Kalmar Union, which it left in 1523. When Sweden entered the Thirty Years' War on the Protestant side its territories expanded, forming the Swedish Empire, which controlled much of the Baltic Sea and remained one of the great powers of Europe until the early 18th century. Most conquered territories outside the peninsula were lost in the 18th and 19th centuries, and the eastern half of Sweden, present-day Finland, passed to Imperial Russia in 1809. In 1814 Sweden forced Norway into a personal union by military means, the last war in which it was directly involved; the union lasted until 1905.

Sweden is a constitutional monarchy and a parliamentary democracy, with a 349-member unicameral Riksdag. Under the 1974 Instrument of Government the king has no formal political power. The country is divided into 21 counties and 290 municipalities, and its Nordic welfare system provides universal health care. Its population is about 10.6 million, and five minority groups are officially recognised: Jews, Romani, Sámi, Sweden Finns and Tornedalians. Sweden joined the European Union in 1995 and NATO in 2024.
switzerland: Switzerland covers 41,291 square kilometres between the Alps, the Swiss Plateau and the Jura Mountains. The Alps make up about 60% of the area, while most of the population lives on the plateau, where cities such as Zurich, Geneva, Basel and Bern stand. Glaciers cover 1,063 square kilometres, and the headwaters of the Rhine, Inn, Ticino and Rhône rise there; the springs of the Rhône and the Rhine are only about 22 kilometres apart, although one river reaches the Mediterranean Sea and the other the North Sea. The country has more than 1500 lakes, among them Lake Geneva, Lake Constance and Lake Maggiore.

The oldest traces of hominids in Switzerland date to about 150,000 years ago, and the oldest known farming settlements, at Gächlingen, to around 5300 BCE. The La Tène culture developed from around 450 BCE, and the Helvetii, one of its most prominent tribes, held the Swiss Plateau.

In 58 BCE they left it, under the influence of the aristocrat Orgetorix, and were defeated by Julius Caesar at the Battle of Bibracte, after which Caesar forced them back to their lands. In 15 BCE Tiberius and his brother Drusus conquered the Alps for the Roman Empire. Towns such as Aventicum and Augusta Raurica reached a considerable size in the first and second centuries CE.

The Old Swiss Confederacy arose in the Late Middle Ages as a defensive and commercial alliance, and the Federal Charter of 1291 is regarded as its founding document. Its independence from the Holy Roman Empire was formally recognised in the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. Revolutionary France invaded in 1798 and imposed the centralist Helvetic Republic, which Napoleon abolished in 1803, reinstating a confederation. After 1830 liberal and conservative movements came into conflict, and the constitution of 1848 created the present federal system.

Switzerland is a federal republic of 26 cantons, with Bern as the federal city. The Federal Assembly has two houses, the Council of States with 46 members and the National Council with 200, and the executive is the seven-member Federal Council. Citizens may challenge laws passed by parliament through optional referendums. The country has four principal linguistic regions, German, French, Italian and Romansh, and about 9 million people. It has followed a policy of armed neutrality since the 16th century, joined the United Nations in 2002 and hosts many international institutions.
sydney: Sydney is a coastal basin, with the Tasman Sea to the east, the Blue Mountains to the west, the Hawkesbury River to the north and the Woronora Plateau to the south. The urban area surrounds Sydney Harbour and extends about 60 kilometres from the Pacific Ocean to the escarpment of the Blue Mountains. The Cumberland Plain, relatively flat, lies to the south and west of the harbour, and the Hornsby Plateau, cut by steep valleys, lies to the north. The flat southern areas were developed first, and the northern reaches became more heavily populated only after the Sydney Harbour Bridge was built. About seventy surf beaches lie along the coast.

The first people in the area were Aboriginal Australians. Flaked pebbles in Western Sydney's gravel might indicate human presence 45,000 to 50,000 years ago, and radiocarbon dating shows human activity from around 30,000 years ago. Before the British arrived there were 4,000 to 8,000 Aboriginal people in the region, living by fishing, hunting and gathering plants and shellfish. Greater Sydney covers the traditional lands of 28 known clans, among them the Gadigal, whose territory along the southern shore of Port Jackson includes the site of the first British settlement.

In 1788 Captain Arthur Phillip, the first governor of New South Wales, named the cove Sydney Cove after Home Secretary Thomas Townshend, 1st Viscount Sydney; its Aboriginal name was Warrane. The population was under 1,000 in 1788 and almost tripled in ten years to 2,953 with convict transportation. The first five governors had near autocratic power. Governor Macquarie set ambitious standards for building, and the convict Francis Greenway, pardoned in 1818, designed the Hyde Park Barracks in 1819. Sydney was declared a city in 1842, when an elected municipal council was set up. New South Wales achieved responsible government in 1856, and in 1901, with the federation of the Australian colonies, Sydney became the capital of the state.

Greater Sydney consists of 658 suburbs spread across 33 local government areas, and the 2021 census recorded a population of 5,231,150. The Australian Museum, opened in 1827, remains Australia's oldest natural history museum, and the Museum of Sydney stands on the site of the first Government House. The Sydney Opera House is World Heritage listed. Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park holds around 1,500 pieces of Aboriginal rock art, the largest cluster of Indigenous sites in Australia.
syria: The modern state of Syria covers 185,180 km2 in the Eastern Mediterranean and the Levant. Its land runs from the Mediterranean coastal plains to the mountains of the west, where Mount Hermon, at 2,814 metres, is the highest point, and much of the centre and east is arid plateau and desert. The valleys of the Euphrates, Orontes and Khabur rivers support agriculture and settlement. Commercial petroleum was first discovered in the northeast in 1956.

The name Syria is borrowed from Ancient Greek, which took it from Luwian sura/i-, attested in the 8th century BCE, and mainstream scholarship relates it to Assyria. From the Seleucid Empire the Greeks applied it to the Levant without distinguishing the Assyrians of Mesopotamia from the Arameans of the Levant. Under the Roman Empire the larger Syria was divided into provinces such as Judaea, renamed Palaestina in 135 CE, and Phoenice, established in 194.

The Natufian culture became sedentary around the 11th millennium BCE, and the site of Tell Qaramel has round stone towers dated to 10650 BCE. The earliest recorded indigenous civilization was the Kingdom of Ebla, near present-day Idlib, which appears to have been founded around 3500 BCE and grew rich through trade with Sumer, Assyria and Akkad and contact with Egypt.

One of its early texts, the Treaty between Ebla and Abarsal of about 2300 BCE, is a trading agreement. Ebla was weakened by a long war with Mari, and in the first half of the 23rd century BCE the conquests of Sargon of Akkad and Naram-Sin ended its domination of Syria.

The modern state emerged from a French Mandate. It gained de jure independence in 1945 as a founding member of the United Nations, and French troops withdrew in April 1946. Coups and coup attempts followed between 1949 and 1971, and a union with Egypt lasted from 1958 to 1961. The Ba'ath Party took power in 1963. Hafez al-Assad came to power in 1970 and was succeeded on his death in 2000 by his son Bashar. A civil war began in 2011, and the Assad government fell in December 2024.
